endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: When a patient opts out, the request is documented in the internal system(s) and flagged for the care team.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether accessible-format AI transparency materials improve understanding or access for patients with disabilities, and no study documents the hazard. The single endorsing source addresses documentation of patient opt-outs rather than accessible formats, so support for this recommendation rests on inference rather than direct evidence.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated without direct tests. The one endorsement, a CHAI framework, states that opt-out requests should be documented and flagged for the care team. That statement does not speak to material formats or disability access.

The only supplied source is a voluntary governance framework using "should" language, and its quoted text concerns opt-out documentation. The supplied material contains no endorsement that directly addresses accessible formats for AI disclosures. Administrators may therefore find that this recommendation lacks a source-specific basis in the evidence map and must justify it on other grounds.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether patients with visual, hearing, cognitive, or motor disabilities can locate, read, and understand AI transparency materials, or whether providing alternative formats such as screen-reader-compatible text, large print, audio, sign language video, or plain-language versions changes comprehension, opt-out rates, or trust. Studies are also needed to document how often current AI disclosures fail basic accessibility checks.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Patients with disabilities who also have limited English proficiency or low literacy may face compounded barriers, and the absence of data means health systems cannot yet judge which formats reach these groups.
